Pele Yoetz 372:1: Shishah (Six) — Regarding the number six, the kabbalists wrote that one must be very careful to say “Hashishi” [“the sixth”, with the definite article], which represents the union of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence; and likewise one must be careful in writing as well — for example, when writing a date on the sixth day, it should be written “on the sixth day” [with the definite article], and when writing chapters, it should be written “the sixth chapter,” and anything similar to this — one should always be careful about this, and especially when reciting the Levites' song, one should say “today is the sixth day” [with the definite article], and intend to unite the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Divine Presence, Yesod and Malchut, and these are ancient matters.
Pele Yoetz 373:1: Serarah (Authority/Leadership) — Authority is a trouble that buries its possessors, since it readily inclines one to become proud and to impose excessive fear upon the congregation not for the sake of Heaven, and it readily leads one to do several improper things and treat the honor of the individual and the many lightly, and the like. Therefore, whoever desires life should flee from authority, and in a place where there is no one else and one is compelled to exercise authority, let him gather strength not to become proud, and in his heart let him humble himself and recognize his limited worth and be despicable and loathsome in his own eyes, and be careful of everyone's honor. And if he needs to display sternness, let him weigh his actions with a scale and balances of justice to act in a manner fitting the need of the hour, and let all his deeds be for the sake of Heaven, and let him not rely on his own understanding — “one who heeds counsel is wise” (Proverbs 12:15), “and salvation is in an abundance of counselors” (ibid. 11:14). And let him pour out his soul before the Name, that He rectify him with good counsel from before Him, so that no mishap result from his hand and that he not become proud — perhaps thereby there is hope that he shall fulfill his obligation and find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man, and shall surely live.
Pele Yoetz 374:1: Sho'el (Borrower) — One who borrows without the owner's knowledge is a robber, and even regarding a fellow's book, it is forbidden to take it and study from it without his permission, and whoever does so, thinking he performs a commandment, has a transgression in his hand instead. And people stumble in this regarding shoes, when being in a group and one goes outside and takes his fellow's shoes. And likewise one who borrows an item or a book from his fellow and lends it to another without the owner's permission is a robber, for the borrower is not permitted to lend it further. And it is good for a man to acquire everything he needs and not need to borrow from his fellow, for sometimes the lender does not wish to lend, and out of embarrassment he lends it, and there is a trace of robbery involved; and sometimes he lies and says, “I have none,” when he does have it, and it turns out he causes his fellow to sin.
Pele Yoetz 374:2: And how much more so must one be careful not to ask anyone for a gift, and one must be concerned lest he gives it out of embarrassment, in which case there is an element of robbery involved. And how much more so from one who does not wish to give — if one takes from him against his will, it is outright robbery. And there are many bad people who take against their fellows' will, and it seems to them as though permitted, not knowing that this is like a robber who goes out on the road and robs and extorts. And likewise in this manner, one who borrows with the intention not to repay — this and that are one and the same. And if people see a person who goes astray and robs and extorts and pillages his fellow creatures, they scorn him and curse him and call him unclean, unclean; but one who takes a gift or something cheap, or borrows with the intention not to repay, it seems to him as though permitted, and his heart does not ache, since he does not know what the prohibition is — may the Good Name grant atonement for it. And though they said (Ketubot 49b) that they compel charity, this means that others compel the wealthy to give for the needs of the poor, but the poor themselves and the sages themselves have no permission to take without the owner's knowledge and without his good will, since there is robbery and desecration of the Name involved, and “whoever hates gifts shall live” (Proverbs 15:27) (and I have already written of this above under the entry Gezel and under the entry Matan — see there).
Pele Yoetz 374:3: And the commandment of lending is a great kindness — “wealth and riches are in his house, and his righteousness endures forever” (Psalms 112:3). And even if his item is somewhat damaged, he gains far more than he loses in the reward he receives from the Name for the kindness, and he shall also be clothed in blessings from the borrower. And every man should instruct his wife to be generous, and acquire extra items in his house in order to lend them, and let them not turn away a borrower empty-handed, and the Lord shall repay them sevenfold into their bosom.
Pele Yoetz 375:1: Sho'el KaInyan (Asking Appropriately) — We have learned (Avot 2:6): the bashful one does not learn. And it is among the traits of the wise man that regarding what he has not heard, he says, “I have not heard,” and he asks appropriately. And one must have understanding in how to ask, for they said in the holy Zohar that a certain child was punished in the heavenly academy for having embarrassed his teacher with his questions. And they said in the Talmud (Mo'ed Katan 5a) that a certain student would ask his teacher questions all year, but on the Shabbat of the festival he would not ask him, since his teacher was busy and might not be able to answer, and this might cause him embarrassment; regarding him they applied the verse (Psalms 50:23), “And to him who orders his way rightly I shall show the salvation of God.” Behold, therefore, one needs a scale of judgment not to ask a sage in front of many people, and especially a visiting guest who has come to town should not be asked questions unless it is established that he is a great man and no secret is beyond him. And whoever has access to a great sage in his town, or when he hears that a sage is coming to town, should not tire or grow weary of asking him all his questions and all his difficulties, and should do nothing, small or great, without asking a sage and without a sage's counsel, so that he act wisely in what he does — then he shall succeed in his ways and then he shall have understanding. And if he asked a sage and the sage did not know how to answer, or answered improperly, he should not challenge him or speak excessively about it, but rather accept everything.
Pele Yoetz 375:2: And especially in the presence of householders, great understanding is needed among Torah scholars, so that one not glorify himself through his fellow's disgrace, to show that he is wise and his fellow is not wise. And if his fellow does not know how to conduct himself in this manner, let him agree that his fellow remain honored and wise in his own eyes and in the eyes of the masses, while he himself is scorned and disdained, and through this the honor of Heaven shall increase, and his own honor shall also increase. And they should not disgrace one another with words, which leads to conflict and desecration of the Name and hatred and rivalry, but rather speak their words calmly, with honor, with proper conduct, and when one does not accept his fellow's words, they should not speak excessively or persist in dispute, but rather each should remain with his own reasoning, and if he erred, let his error rest with him, and let them turn to another matter. And especially regarding matters of a sermon, one does not respond to the sermon (Pa'aneach Raza on Toldot Yitzchak), and to whatever any Torah scholar says, let him answer “Amen” and “we agree, we agree,” and say, “The matter is good.” And especially in front of the masses, great understanding is needed not to grieve or humiliate a Torah scholar. These are some of the paths of Torah scholars who increase peace in the world; let the wise man hear and add learning.
Pele Yoetz 376:1: The letter Tav: Tefillin — Tefillin require a clean body, that one not sleep in them and not pass gas while wearing them. And the halachic authorities wrote (Orach Chaim, sec. 38, para. 2) that if it is clear to him that he cannot withstand it without passing gas, and the time for prayer is passing, it is better that the time for prayer pass and he complete it with the prayer following it, rather than pray with an unclean body or pass gas while wearing tefillin. And preparation is needed, for they said (Berachot 15a) that one who wishes to accept upon himself the complete yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven should relieve himself, wash his hands, put on tefillin, and pray. And they said (ibid.) that whoever does these things, Scripture accounts it to him as though he built an altar and offered a sacrifice upon it. Therefore let him not be lazy and not fail to relieve himself and examine himself well before prayer, and through this he shall not come to pass gas during his prayer while wearing tefillin.
Pele Yoetz 376:2: And likewise regarding sleep, preparation is needed: if he rose at the head of the watches, or was awake at night and sees that the bonds of sleep are falling upon him, let him lie down and rest a little at the morning watch, so that sleep not overtake him during prayer while wearing tefillin. And if he is standing in prayer and dozing, let him stand on his feet and walk about, and let him sniff powder that induces sneezing into his nostrils, and gather strength like a man not to sleep during prayer and while wearing tefillin, and according to the pain is the reward. And likewise one must be exceedingly careful not to let his mind wander from the tefillin, and the Ari, of blessed memory, was exceedingly strict about this. And at the very least, whenever he can, back and forth, let him touch the tefillin every hour. And especially one must guard exceedingly against thoughts of women, for the halachic authorities wrote (Orach Chaim, sec. 38, para. 4) that if it is clear to him that he cannot withstand it without thoughts of women, it is better for him not to put on tefillin. And if at every hour a person is obligated to push away bad thoughts with both hands, how much more so at the time the tefillin are upon him.
Pele Yoetz 376:3: And the other detailed laws of tefillin are written in the compendiums of the halachic authorities. I shall only mention this here: many of the common people think they are wearing tefillin, yet they are among those of whom it is said that they do not wear tefillin at all, since they are not careful to place them in their proper place, placing the head tefillin too low, over the eyes — this is the way of heretics, and they do not fulfill the obligation of tefillin, and one must inform them. And likewise there are many who place the head straps in the middle of the head, close together, and this is not the straight way; rather, they must be fastened tightly around the head. And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 14b) that whoever recites the Shema without tefillin is as though he bears false witness.
Pele Yoetz 376:4: And the merit of tefillin is so great that it is said of them (Deuteronomy 28:10), “And all the peoples of the earth shall see that the Name of the Lord is called upon you, and they shall fear you.” And how greatly have some travelers erred, who cease wearing tefillin because of the mockery of the gentiles — this is a great folly, to nullify a Torah commandment because of the gentiles' mockery. Is it not known that since we are in exile, our enemies mock us, we have become a disgrace to our neighbors, mockery and derision to those around us? What does the mockery of the complacent matter to us — shall our flesh pain us because of it? Is it not fitting for us to endure even physical pain and even the giving of one's life for the honor of our Creator, how much more so mockery, which one should not be concerned about at all? And a person should always be bold as a leopard to do the will of our Father in Heaven, and how much more so on the road, especially regarding the commandment of tefillin, whose segulah is that all the peoples of the earth shall fear him, and this is what travelers seek. And likewise regarding all the commandments and the precise details taught by the Sages, travelers must be especially careful, for all roads are presumed dangerous, and Satan prosecutes at a time of danger. And “whoever guards a commandment shall know no evil thing” (Ecclesiastes 8:5), only good, and the Lord shall call him “peace.”
Pele Yoetz 377:1: Torah — Who can tell the praise of Torah, for its merchandise is better than the merchandise of silver, and as we have learned (Kiddushin 82a), Rabbi Nehorai says: I set aside all the trades in the world and teach my son only Torah, etc. And the Talmud, the Midrashim, the holy Zohar, and all the holy books are already full of splendor, speaking of the praise of Torah, and well-known matters need no proof, and the whole world knows and testifies and declares that Torah is great and its greatness is beyond investigation; but no one takes it to heart to give his life and his very strength to teach his sons Torah as is fitting to do.
Pele Yoetz 377:2: And whoever wishes to grant his sons merit toward the crown of Torah must strive on their behalf from the womb and from conception, that the parents sanctify themselves during relations and think of the great ones of the generations, and their heart shall cry out to their Father in Heaven to give them holy seed, seed of men perfect in traits and knowledge, wise and learned. And let him always pray to the Name before conception and after conception and birth; let father and mother never cease prayer from their mouths, and let them distribute money to Torah scholars and ask them to pray for their offspring. And during pregnancy the woman should strive to hear the sound of Torah, and likewise after birth they should place the newborn in a place of Torah, as they said regarding what we have learned (Avot 2:8): Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananiah — happy is she who bore him, for his mother caused him to become a great sage, since while pregnant with him she would go to the study house to hear words of Torah, and would say to the sages, “Pray for the child in my womb, that he be wise.” And when she gave birth, she took his cradle to the study house so that he hear words of Torah and they be established in his mind.
Pele Yoetz 377:3: And the masters of ethics have already warned with extraordinary caution not to sing to the baby when it cries with foreign songs and songs of frivolous flirtation, for it injures the child's soul; rather, if one wishes to sing to quiet it, let him sing to it snippets of Torah. And it grieves me, the custom found in some places, that when a woman gives birth, on some day during that week they call the women of the city to make a visit, and they sing there foreign songs and songs of frivolous flirtation; and likewise on the night of guarding the son, that is, the night of the circumcision, in a place where the newborn should hear the voice of Torah, he instead hears the voice of foreign songs and songs of frivolous flirtation — and this causes, through our sins, many foolish sons, destructive sons, unreliable sons, to be found, since they were conceived in sin. Let one who guards his soul distance himself from this, and never allow this to be done in his house, as I have written above under the entry Shir, and how much more so in the presence of the newborn child.
Pele Yoetz 377:4: And when the child grows a little and is a small child who knows how to speak, his father shall teach him Torah, and every day and every hour say with him verses of Torah and matters of Torah. When he grows a little more, let him take him to a children's teacher, and always, when he studies with a children's teacher, the study at home is the essential thing. And every day and every night and every Shabbat and every time he is free, let him study with the child according to his ability, and if he is not capable of this — since the child has already grown in Torah and he cannot study with him, or he has no free time to study with him, or the man is not in his house — let him allot a portion of money for some Torah scholar, or let the poor man speak supplications to some Torah scholar to study with him at appointed times. And it is true that money answers everything, but whoever has no money should have the currency of teaching his sons himself, or of pouring out his soul before every Torah scholar in the city. And if there is no Torah scholar in the city, let him go into exile with his sons to a place of Torah, and lick the dust of the sages' feet, until they have mercy on him and teach his sons Torah.
Pele Yoetz 377:5: But the evil of man on earth is that they do not know how great is the evil of the common person, for it is great: they toil in this world with great toil and effort, on the roads, mountains and hills, seas and rivers, eating the bread of sorrow, going from evil to evil, walking in darkness, permitting what is forbidden and forbidding what is permitted, and the light of Torah does not shine upon them, and they rise early and stay late for idle and forbidden matters, and spend their days in vanity and their years in confusion, until they run to the pit of destruction — woe to them in this world, alas for them in the World to Come. Not so the Torah scholars: it is good for them in this world and they shall delight in abundance for their souls in the World to Come, for they shall live a life of tranquility, since “Torah brings its bread from afar,” and they conduct themselves with good traits and uprightness, and remove anger and sadness from their hearts and evil from their flesh, and are not resentful about anything in the world, and their flesh dwells securely, and great is study that leads to action (Megillah 27a; Kiddushin 40b), in such a way that they run toward the life of the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 377:6: Behold, therefore, the man who is pure and has seen or known the praise of Torah, and his flesh pains him and his soul mourns over him for not having merited to have his portion among those who sit in the study house, should have regard for his sons' souls and give his life for all his sons, that at least one of them be a Torah scholar, and at the very least he should not let them be common, ignorant people, but rather they should be learned and full of fear of the Name. And he has regard not only for his sons' souls, but also for his own soul, spirit, and higher soul, for great is the benefit sons bring to their father when they are Torah scholars, through their Torah and their service of the blessed Name. And since they are Torah scholars, they are careful about their father's honor in his life and in his death, and always, all their days, do all that is in their power for his repose and the elevation of his soul, in such a way that they raise him up from Gehinnom and save him from all judgments and elevate him level upon level, until he stands in the company of the righteous, as told in several stories in the Midrashim. And had a person been given permission to return from that world after seeing the manner and judgment of the World to Come, he would become a perfectly righteous man and would truly give his life to teach his sons Torah. And he has regard not only for his sons' souls and his own soul, but the essential thing is that a person have regard for his Maker's honor, for this is the entire fruit that a person should desire in sons: that they do their Maker's will, workers of truth, to give satisfaction to our Creator, for otherwise what do sons give or add — and if they are bad sons, their absence is better than the presence of evil.
Pele Yoetz 377:7: And one who deepens this, to do these things for the sake of Heaven, to give satisfaction to our Creator specifically, should find it almost equal in his eyes to teach his own son Torah as to teach his fellow's son — this and that are the same, giving satisfaction to his Creator, and a person does not know which shall succeed, and the essential “sons” are the students. And though his own sons come before his fellow's sons, happy is the man who holds to this and also to that, for perhaps the students shall succeed more than his sons, and he shall rejoice in them. And it is known how greatly our sages, of blessed memory, elaborated (Sanhedrin 19b) on the praise of one who teaches his fellow's son Torah, that it is as though he fathered him, and that he merits to sit in the academy on high, and even if the Holy One, blessed be He, decrees a decree, he annuls it. And how greatly they elaborated in the holy Zohar on the reward and praise that comes to one who grants merit to a hidden [soul, i.e., an unlearned person] — greater than this is one who teaches his own sons and his fellow's sons Torah, for the light within it returns them to the good.
Pele Yoetz 377:8: And Torah scholars who do not wish to teach their own sons and young students, because it seems to them like neglecting the study house, since when they study for themselves they can study several pages of Talmud and halachic authorities in one day and compose their own novel Torah insights — not so with students, where one must spend time and time again reviewing with them until they learn each matter, requiring great effort, toil, and labor — have not done well. And whoever's deeds are for the sake of Heaven, to give satisfaction to our Creator, for this must be our entire aim during our lifetime, to spend our lives giving satisfaction before Him, blessed be His Name, should not be concerned about any of this, but rather choose whatever gives greater satisfaction to our Creator, and he gives more and more satisfaction to his Creator by teaching his fellow's son and his own son even the alphabet, vanity without sin, than by studying the laws of leprosy and tents [difficult, less practically urgent areas], and “if there are no goats, there are no billy-goats” [without students there are no future teachers] (see Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 10:2), and there is a time for every purpose, and according to the pain is the reward, and it is fitting to fulfill through this, “And you shall love your neighbor as yourself” — this is a great principle in the Torah. For just as, if he were not capable of teaching his own sons, he would want others to have regard for him and teach his sons Torah, so he must have regard for others and teach their sons Torah, and especially if they have no father, let him have mercy on the orphans and on their father's soul, and imagine as though their father were pleading with him to save him from a flame of fire, and when the man's soul finds rest through him, there is no greater true kindness than this, performed for the living and for the dead, and his reward is doubled and redoubled from Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 377:9: And our sages, of blessed memory, already said: be careful with the children of the poor, for from them Torah shall issue (Nedarim 81a). Be careful with the children of the common people, for from them Torah shall issue (Sanhedrin 96a). And the leaders of cities, in every city, are obligated to strive greatly for the study of Torah with all their soul and all their might, and appoint children's teachers for every level of study, and appoint proper, respectable people as overseers who shall check on the children every week to see the order of their studies, and ensure that the teachers do their work, the work of Heaven, faithfully, and encourage the children with both blows and good words and rewards and gifts, so that they advance in levels in the order of study. And it is known how great is the merit of the breath of the children in the house of their teacher, to the point that they said (Shabbat 119b) that the world is sustained by the breath of the children in the house of their teacher, and they annul all harsh and evil decrees, and one does not interrupt the children in the house of their teacher even for the building of the Holy Temple (ibid.), and many other such merits are said regarding the study of children in the house of their teacher. Behold, therefore, given the greatness of the commandments and the benefit that follows from it, it is fitting for the leaders of cities to strengthen themselves in this with all their soul and all their might to raise up the banner of the Torah, and not to be concerned about all the effort and expense, given the abundant good they do for their own souls and the satisfaction they give their Creator.
Pele Yoetz 377:10: And this is a great principle: a person should not despair of mercy, in the manner of some people who say, “This son will certainly not turn out to be a scholar, and if we leave him to Torah study he will be bald on this side and bald on that [i.e., accomplish nothing], so it would be better to send him into business, that he learn to bring sustenance to his house” — this is vanity, for whoever sits and studies Torah shall certainly profit and not lose, for if he does not turn out to be a scholar, at least he shall be learned and not a common, ignorant person, while to learn to be a merchant requires no wisdom or time, for he shall learn it quickly, and money moves of itself, and it is possible his work shall be done through others.
Pele Yoetz 377:11: And if a man is poor and cannot feed his sons, let him suffer a little with them and teach them Torah until they grow up, and the Torah shall stand by them to feed and support them with good sustenance, permitted, at ease, comfortably, honorably — for even if they do not reach the level of great sages, halachic authorities in Israel, in any case they can be cantors and children's teachers and be among the righteous of the many, numerous as the stars, and be engaged in the work of Heaven, and their portion shall be among those who sit in the study house and not among those who sit at street corners. And it is true that the world cannot exist without merchants, and if everyone were a scholar, then there would be no bread for scholars, since the Torah was not given to eaters of manna, and the Holy One, blessed be He, no longer rains bread from heaven; but they already said (Kiddushin 82a): the world cannot exist without a perfumer and without a tanner — happy is he whose trade is perfumery, woe to him whose trade is tanning. So the world cannot exist without scholars and without merchants, teachers, and cantors — happy is he whose work is the work of Heaven, and happy is he whose portion is among those who sit in the study house. And every person should say (ibid. 82a): I set aside all the trades in the world and teach my son only Torah. And if the world needs merchants, it is possible for the world to be sustained through others.
Pele Yoetz 377:12: And the man who is a merchant and whose time has passed for being among those who sit in the study house should do what is in his power to do and let his desire be in the Torah of the Name; whenever he is free, let him study what he knows, or go to the sages to hear teachings in order to observe, do, and fulfill, and let him not fail to pray with the congregation the morning, afternoon, and evening prayers and to fix times for Torah day and night, and let him give his life for his sons to become Torah scholars, and let him support those who study Torah, for like the portion of one who guards the equipment and like the portion of one who goes down to battle, portion for portion they share alike, and great is the deed, as we find with Zebulun, who preceded Issachar; and let him do every good thing he can, and fear every sin as one fears a sword, and let all his deeds be for the sake of Heaven. If he does thus, great is the benefit from his own toil — happy is he in this world, and it is well with him in the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 377:13: And we have learned (Avot 6:2): woe to creatures for the insult to the Torah. And the commentators explained that one who studies Torah is considered like one who is told, “Count out gold coins, and whatever you count, take for yourself as much as you can” — certainly he would not tire or grow weary of counting continuously all day and all night, and if he is lazy and does not count, he disgraces the gold coins and admits they are not important in his eyes — so it is with this matter. And they further explained that the insult to the Torah is that whoever does not engage in Torah is called “rebuked” (Shemot Rabbah 41:7), and this shows that the Torah is so despised in his eyes that he agrees to be rebuked, that is, under a ban, rather than engage in Torah — there is no greater insult than this. And even if a person studies all day and all night, but wishes to free himself for idleness for just half an hour, to engage in gambling or idle words and be among those who sit at street corners, this does not exempt him from the Day of Judgment. And as Rabbi Yishmael said (Menachot 99b) to his nephew who asked him, after he had studied the entire Torah, whether it was permitted for him to learn Greek wisdom, he said to him: it is written (Joshua 1:8), “And you shall meditate on it day and night” — go and find an hour that is neither day nor night, and learn Greek wisdom then. How much more so we, orphans of orphans, lacking in knowledge, for we have grown exceedingly poor, and it is written (Job 7:19), “You do not let me alone even to swallow my spittle,” and our holy sages, of blessed memory, whom we believe are true and whose words are true, explained that even for the brief time it takes to swallow saliva, a person is destined to give an account and shall be asked how he spent it. Woe to us from the Day of Judgment and from the depth of judgment, and over this and the like, hearts ache: how the reins have been loosened and how Torah has been forgotten and has become treated as permitted even by some Torah scholars and many of the common people, wasting precious time, many hours, in gambling and idle and forbidden words, and therefore “the harvest has passed, the summer has ended” (Jeremiah 8:20), and we have not been saved — the Lord is righteous, for our sages, of blessed memory, said regarding the verse (Micah 1:5), “All this is for the transgression of Jacob,” that all the troubles and evils that come upon the world, general and specific, and the delay of the Messiah, are all because of the sin of neglecting Torah.
Pele Yoetz 377:14: Behold, therefore, to you, men, I call, children of the living God: let us be strong and strengthen ourselves for our God, and have regard for our Maker's honor and for our soul, spirit, and higher soul, and let us not destroy ourselves knowingly, and let us believe in our holy Torah and in the words of our holy sages, of blessed memory, and from now on let us not waste precious time in idleness; rather, when we lie down and when we rise let us speak of Torah, and rejoice and exult in words of Torah study and commandments, and meditate on them day and night — perhaps God shall be entreated for us and cause His redemption to sprout and bring His Messiah near. And let not the merchant say, “What further obligation do I have? Behold, I have studied so many psalms, so much of the holy Zohar, Ma'amadot, and the like, and I have already grown weary, for one who is a Torah scholar can engage in Torah all day, but with these studies it is impossible to be engaged all day” — this too is vanity, for our sages, of blessed memory, said (Tanna DeVei Eliyahu Zuta, ch. 2): whoever does not know how to study, if he repeats all day the verse (Genesis 36:22), “And Lotan's sister was Timna,” it is considered before the Omnipresent as though he were engaged in the laws of leprosy and tents. And this excuse does not exempt him from judgment; rather, let him toil and repeat his study even a thousand times, and let him not sit idle regarding the honor of the blessed Name and the honor of His Torah. And behold, whoever hears this and the like, matters that many have trampled upon and treated as permitted, shall think it is an impossible thing to fulfill, to be separated from this world like ministering angels; but would that I could find it written in some book that the Name shall not bring judgment upon these matters — I too would remain silent, but I grieve for myself and for our brothers, the children of Israel, for I fear before the wrath, and the poured-out fury that rests upon the heads of the wicked shall fall upon any matter of transgression on the great, awesome, and fearsome Day of Judgment — who can bear it? Therefore, out of my great grief, I have spoken thus far to myself, and let the listener listen, and upon him shall come the blessing of good, and all beginnings are hard, and according to the pain is the reward.
Pele Yoetz 377:15: And how good is the portion of women, who are clean of this sin of neglecting Torah; but they too shall bear their portion if they are the cause of their husbands and sons neglecting Torah study — woe to them, alas for them. And upon them rests this commandment: to have their husbands and sons called up to read the Torah (Berachot 17a), and especially the wife of a Torah scholar must drive sleep from her eyes and rise while it is still night and awaken her husband and prepare the fire and coffee for him and attend to him and serve him. And every woman must also strive with her husband that he engage in Torah on winter nights and on Shabbatot and festivals and at every free time. And she must also strive greatly with her sons that they engage in Torah, and press herself greatly with the household needs so that her sons and husband engage in Torah with a settled mind, for one hour is better [than more with a confused mind], and let her do all that is in her power to do so that her husband and sons study. Whoever does these things shall be blessed among women in the tent, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (ibid.): great is the promise the Holy One, blessed be He, made to women, greater than to men — “Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her own works praise her in the gates” (Proverbs 31:31).
Pele Yoetz 377:16: And whoever engages in Torah is thereby elevated, for great is study that leads to action (Kiddushin 40b), and study is not the essential thing but rather action. “The beginning of wisdom is fear of the Lord; good understanding to all who practice them” (Avot 1:17; Psalms 111:10). Therefore let a person choose to study or hear teachings on necessary laws, and be exceedingly careful to observe and fulfill them according to the Torah and according to the words of our holy sages, of blessed memory, not turning right or left, for this is the whole of man, and through this he shall merit to live and inherit good and blessing in this world and the World to Come, and truly they said (Peah 1:1): Torah study is equal to them all.
Pele Yoetz 378:1: Temimut (Wholeness/Innocence) — It is written (Deuteronomy 18:13), “You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God.” And it is written (Proverbs 10:9), “He who walks in innocence walks securely.” And through this Jacob our father, peace be upon him, was praised, as it is written (Genesis 25:27), “And Jacob was a wholesome man,” and likewise regarding Job (Job 1:1), “a wholesome and upright man.” The matter of wholeness is that one should not strive to know the future through lots, witchcraft, and the like, and should not grieve over tomorrow's trouble, but rather cast his burden upon the Lord. And he should not strive to know what is in his fellow's heart, and should not walk in the way of shrewdness and deceit to incline after profit, but rather walk in his innocence, righteous, and not think of the affairs of this world and the affairs of his livelihood, but let his desire be in the Torah of the Lord, and meditate on it day and night (Psalms 1:2), and the Lord shall not withhold good from those who walk in innocence, and those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.
Pele Yoetz 379:1: Talmidim (Students) — We have learned (Avot 1:1): and raise up many students. And our sages, of blessed memory, said regarding the verse (Ecclesiastes 11:6), “In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not withhold your hand” — if he had students in his youth, let him have students in his old age, for you do not know which will succeed, this or that, or whether both alike will be good. And great wisdom is needed to teach Torah to students according to a child's understanding, to feed it to him like an ox [i.e., digestibly], and this is a craft in itself, requiring that the teacher be expert in which is the straight way to teach students matters according to their level, in such a way that a little sustains much, and the matters become established in their minds and hearts, and he should not be satisfied that they merely learn things superficially, but rather that they understand the matters well, in such a way that even if his own mind becomes confused, they shall not become confused and shall be firm in what they learned. And it is not enough that he teach his students Torah, but he should also teach them ethics, fear of the Name, and the paths of uprightness.
Pele Yoetz 379:2: And every person should make himself a student to the holy ones who are in the land, in the manner of the statement of our sages, of blessed memory (Avot 1:12): be among the disciples of Aaron, etc., among the disciples of Abraham our father — as he learns from them, let him do as they did, and through this he shall merit to be his own portion and share with them. And one of the things through which Torah is acquired is through the dialectic of students. And the master said (Ta'anit 7a): I have learned much Torah from my teachers, and more from my colleagues, and more than all from my students. And these are true, and their words are true, and “the righteous shall be tested.” And we have already written of this above under the entries Melamdei Tinokot and Torah.
Pele Yoetz 380:1: Ta'anit (Fasting) — Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Ta'anit 11a): whoever fasts is called holy. And Mahari wrote in the book Tziporen Shamir, section 11, and these are his words: happy is he who can fast over his sins, and the segulot of fasting are many; among them, that the Sitra Achra has no power to attach itself to one engaged in fasting. Through fasting one comes to humility, for he recognizes what man is, since through withholding a little bread his strength wanes. One engaged in fasting does not come into trial, for the blessed Name sees that he tests himself through fasting. He is called a mighty man who conquers his inclination, and it is fitting for the Divine Presence to rest upon him. He has no prosecutor, and his prayer is heard. If he is liable to suffering, he shows that he accepts it with love. There are angels who cannot ascend except through the power of people's fasting. It is the secret of the sacrifice, whose fat and blood began to ascend as a pleasing aroma, as they elaborated at length in the holy Zohar, Parashat Shemot — all these merits and more, as they, of blessed memory, wrote, that is, if through fasting he examines his deeds and returns in repentance and fasts for atonement — thus far his words. And the holy master, author of Reshit Chokhmah, likewise elaborated at length on the obligation of fasting for the sinning soul and on the benefit that follows from it, to the point that whoever reads his words shall desire to fast.
Pele Yoetz 380:2: And through our sins, in this orphaned generation, there is no one found who fasts for the atonement of sins, except a few of the remnant whom the Lord calls, but the rest of the common people, who need fasting most of all, do not wish to fast, and say, “Why should I fast? I have not murdered, I have not committed adultery,” and say jokingly, “Better to eat for ten days than fast for one day,” since fasting is hard for them. And it is a pity that some do not even fast on public fast days, saying it is hard for them and they cannot fast. And this is because “the way of a man is upright in his own eyes,” and he thinks he has no sin he has committed. And even when they know and recognize that they have sinned, transgressed, and rebelled, they do not know its severity and how much evil and blemish it causes through his sins, and how many harsh and bitter punishments and many pains pass over the sinning soul for any matter of transgression, such that if the wicked man were given permission to return from that world after seeing the harsh and bitter punishments, which are exceedingly, exceedingly severe, beyond our own reach while we are in this world, he would agree to afflict his soul day and night all the days of his life to atone for his soul and purify what he blemished and rectify what he distorted, since with a little suffering he accepts upon himself in this world and afflicting his soul willingly, he reduces greatly the punishments of the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 380:3: Go and learn from our holy sages, who knew the severity of sin, and therefore fasted greatly over any sin. King David said (Psalms 109:24), “My knees are weak from fasting.” Rabbi Elazar, for not having protested against his neighbor whose cow used to go out with a strap between its horns [a questionable practice], his teeth blackened from fasting (Yerushalmi Shabbat 5:4). Rabbi Yehoshua, for having said, “I am ashamed of your words, House of Shammai,” his teeth blackened from fasting (Chagigah 22b). Rav Huna's tefillin strap turned over, and he fasted forty fasts (Mo'ed Katan 25a). And so, entire and many people in every generation spend their days in fasts and self-mortifications — how much more so we, who are full of sins and iniquities, bundles upon bundles, such that if we were to live a thousand years and fast all our years, we would not manage to rectify our distortions and purify all our blemishes. And it is true that fasting is hard, but how shall a servant appease his master, and with what shall he atone for the sin — through eating, drinking, and merry company?
Pele Yoetz 380:4: And it is true that the essence of repentance is that one regret the sin with complete regret, and He who knows secrets shall testify regarding him that he has resolved in his heart never to return to folly, as Maimonides wrote (Laws of Repentance, ch. 2, para. 2), to the point that they said (Kiddushin 49b) that one who betroths a woman and says to her, “On condition that I am a perfectly righteous man,” she is betrothed, even if it were known to us that he was a perfectly wicked man, since perhaps he contemplated repentance in his heart — it turns out that through contemplation of repentance alone he becomes a perfectly righteous man. And likewise from what they said regarding the verse (Psalms 93:3), “You humble man unto the dust” — unto the utter dissolution of the soul (Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1).
Pele Yoetz 380:5: And you might raise a difficulty regarding the rectifications of repentance prescribed by our teacher the Ari and the other kabbalists, who required several fasts for each single sin. They have already resolved this: fasts and self-mortifications are needed to remove and restrain the destroyers and prosecutors created through iniquities and transgressions, for whoever commits one transgression acquires for himself one accuser (Avot 4:11), and also to purify what one has blemished. And this is comparable to one whose willfulness of heart carried him, or through his lack of care, to soil the king's palace, and the king hated him greatly for having had the heart to do so; and when he repented and came to the king and fell at his feet, weeping and pleading with him, out of the kindnesses of the pious king he immediately agrees and forgives his guilt and loves him freely, but on condition that he clean up what he soiled in the king's palace, and according to the greatness of the filth and its dryness, so much toil and great effort are needed to clean it, and if the man is lazy about cleaning what he soiled, he shall be punished for not having had regard for the pious king's honor, and in the end he must clean it against his will, not for his own benefit. And there is a further point: that upon the king seeing the man's good will to rectify what he damaged, he too shall send his help so that with little effort he shall rectify it; not so for a man who has no regard for his own honor — the king too shall not have regard for him and shall leave him to prolong his toil until he rectifies what was distorted. So it is with this matter: although the Holy One, blessed be He, is a merciful and gracious King, He said (Hosea 14:3), “Take words with you and return,” etc., “I shall love them freely, for My anger has turned from him” — but in any case one must purify what he blemished above regarding the holy Names, the throne of glory, and the like, and what he damaged in the channels of the flow, and what he created — destroyers to injure — through streams of water flowing from his eyes, and he shall afflict his soul with fasts and self-mortifications and various kinds of afflictions, self-mortifications and sufferings of love that he accepts upon himself of his own good will out of the love he has for his Creator and his regard for His honor, all according to how much guilt he has accumulated and according to how much time has passed without his taking it to heart to rectify what he distorted, as is written under the entry Teshuvah, with the help of Heaven, and the little he does of his own good will is worth much, and the Lord shall send His help — sacred — as it is written (Micah 7:18), “And passes over transgression,” as it is written (Isaiah 4:4), “The Lord shall wash away the filth of the daughters of Zion.” Not so for a man who has no regard for his Maker's honor and does not strive to rectify what he distorted — he too shall be punished for this, and in the end he must rectify his distortion through harsh and bitter sufferings that shall come upon him against his will, not for his own benefit, in this world or the World to Come.
Pele Yoetz 380:6: Behold, therefore, a person is obligated to have regard for his own soul and his Maker's honor, and let him do all that is in his power to do to rectify his distortion before the days of evil come — cleansing sufferings, or death, or the punishments of the World to Come, as our sages, of blessed memory, said regarding the four categories of atonement (Yoma 86a) — for it all depends on the greatness of the sin and its severity and on what kind of person he is, since whoever is greater than his fellow, his sin makes a greater impression and blemish, and it all depends on his knowledge and his inclination — how many distinctions there are, for good or otherwise, and this depends on the weighing of the God of knowledge. In any case, every person should do all that is in his power to do, and let his inclination not persuade him by telling him he has no strength to fast, for this is a well-known falsehood, since we have seen with our own eyes many weak people who afflict their souls with fasts and self-mortifications and are healthier and stronger than those who eat delicacies, for one who comes to purify himself is assisted from Heaven, and man does not live by bread alone, but by every utterance of the Lord's mouth does man live (Deuteronomy 8:3). And beginnings are hard. In any case, an obligation rests upon one to begin fasting, and if he sees that it is likely he shall be seized by a ravenous hunger, Heaven forbid, he may stop, and then he shall have grounds to say he had no strength to fast; but if he ceases fasting because of hunger that is merely hard for him, He who sits in heaven shall laugh and say to him, “I told you, do you wish your sins to be atoned for with a fattened chicken and old wine to eat to satiety? This is impossible.”
Pele Yoetz 380:7: And not only for sins and iniquities must we fast, but also whoever wishes to merit the crown of Torah, for himself or for his sons, must fast, as we find with King Solomon, who fasted forty days to merit wisdom, as they expounded regarding the large Mem at the beginning of Proverbs. And they likewise said in the Talmud (Bava Metzia 85a) that Rav Yosef fasted forty fasts, and another forty, and another hundred, until they read to him (Isaiah 59:21), “They shall not depart from your mouth or from the mouth of your offspring,” etc. How much more so for us, full of sins, whose sins withhold good from us, that we must fast — perhaps God shall be entreated for us.
Pele Yoetz 380:8: And it is true that for one engaged in the work of Heaven, fasting nullifies him from the work of Heaven, and therefore the halachic authorities wrote (Orach Chaim, sec. 571, para. 2) that a children's teacher is not permitted to fast, and especially one who studies with deep analysis — fasting harms him, for he cannot analyze a matter thoroughly, since fasting confuses the mind, and study requires clarity. And the halachic authorities have already disputed whether one whose Torah is his occupation is obligated to fast for his sins even though it nullifies his study, or whether it is perhaps better that he study and his Torah atone for him. And the more accepted view is that he too must fast to restrain transgression, so that his Torah be acceptable. And I say the resolution of the matter is that it is good for a Torah scholar to hold to this and also to that, and in some year or at some time of the year, such as during the days of Elul and the Ten Days of Repentance, and how much more so during Shovavim, let him fast, and if he cannot study with deep analysis, let him study by rote — the holy Zohar, ethical books, Psalms, the order of sacrifices, and the like — and during the rest of the days of his life let him study with deep analysis, and thus both are fulfilled in his hand.
Pele Yoetz 380:9: And it is best that even on the days he eats, he act in such a way that it be counted for him as a fast, that is, like
Pele Yoetz 380:10: what the RaAVaD wrote, that if he withdraws his hand during his meal from some food that is pleasant to him, for atonement of his sins, it is counted for him like a fast and like a sacrifice and an atoning altar. And likewise a person can afflict his soul by not eating meat and not drinking wine on the days when supplications are recited, for the master of Chesed L'Avraham wrote that it is not good to eat meat and drink wine on weekdays, since all the punishment of the beating of the grave is for eating meat and drinking wine on weekdays; or let him not eat meat except at night, as the Torah taught proper conduct, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 75a) regarding the verse (Exodus 16:8), “In the evening, meat to eat.” Or let him eat meat and not eat fruit, or let him fast for a number of hours, as they said (Yerushalmi Nedarim 8:1) regarding Rav Yochanan, who used to say, “I shall be fasting until I leave the study house.” And likewise, if he withdraws his hand from eating fine bread and eats coarse bread, it is considered a fast, as we find with Daniel (Daniel 10:3), who said, “I ate no pleasant bread.” And it is written (ibid.), “From the day you set your heart to fast” — this shows it is called a fast. And likewise in this manner, whatever a person diminishes of the pleasures of this world for the atonement of his sins is called a fast.
